Adding a boil-off capture and utilization system to LH delivery trucks would add complexity to the system and require further 2 investigation before rollout. Further analysis would be needed to determine under what conditions the solutions to mitigate LH losses during tank transfers and during delivery presented in this subsection are 2 economically viable compared to standard practices. 4.2.1.3 Airport Cryogenic Hydrogen Storage Once hydrogen arrives to the airport in a cryogenic state, it would be stored in bulk LH storage 2 tanks. Conventional LH storage tanks are typically cylindrical and vacuum insulated, similar to 2 those used during LH trucking, to limit the effects of boil-off caused by heat transfer. Linde 2 offers cylindrical (or bullet-type) stationary LH tanks up to about 28 metric tons (400 m3 with 2 71 kg LH /m3) in either a horizontal or vertical position (Linde n.d.). As mentioned in Section 2 4.2, the larger the tank, the less hydrogen boil-off that occurs because of the reduced surface- area-to-volume ratio. The shape with the lowest ratio is a sphere, but because of the design and construction complexity of spherical tanks (Fesmire and Swanger 2021), cylindrical tanks are more common. As of 2022, the largest spherical LH storage tank is located at NASA Kennedy 2 Space Center, holding approximately 336 metric tons of LH (4,732 m3 with 71 kg LH /m3). It 2 2 will be used to fuel rockets in support of future moon and Mars missions (Swanger 2022). For reference, standard LH storage tanks of around 4,000 kg typically have a capital cost 2 (equipment plus installation) of about $100/kg–$200/kg (Houchins and James 2022; Argonne National Laboratory n.d.). For larger tanks, there are likely to be economies-of-scale benefits. Similar to LH delivery, boil-off for LH storage is on the order of 0.1% per day to 5% per day 2 2 (Frazer-Nash Consultancy 2022; Clean Energy Group 2025). The exact rate of boil-off is dependent on factors such as ortho-to-para hydrogen conversion, storage tank shape (surface- area-to-volume ratio), and quality of tank insulation. Similar cryogenic fuel handling technology is studied and implemented in stationary storage tanks as in LH tanker trucks. However, it is 2 worth noting that active boil-off management systems for stationary storage are further along than those for LH storage on tanker trucks because of the increased complexity and constraints 2 of mobile storage systems (Fabrum 2024; GenH2 n.d.-b). In addition, boil-off gas capture and compressor systems could be more easily integrated with stationary storage than mobile LH 2 delivery storage, and there is potential to be multiple end-use applications for the boil-off gas directly at the airport (e.g., power generation, ground support equipment, gaseous-hydrogen- powered aircraft). 4.2.1.4 Airport Cryogenic Hydrogen Dispensing For dispensing hydrogen, fixed stations directly next to bulk storage or mobile refueling stations are nearer-term solutions than hydrant systems.
